Motivation According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the building sector (residential, public, and commercial) currently accounts for 30% of the global energy consumption and 28% of the worldwide carbon dioxide (CO ) emissions (Figure 1(a)) [1]. Space heating 2 accounts for 45% of building emissions, whilst space cooling consumes 20% of global electrical demand [1], [2]. As urban development expands and decarbonization efforts continue, the demand for electrical space heating and cooling systems is expected to increase. This will put more pressure on the electrical grid, especially during peak demands, and relying partially on wind and solar energy may lead to unstable supply and higher costs to meet those peak needs, e.g., the duck curve in California (Figure 1(b)). Thus, exploring avenues such as energy storage systems and improving the grid reliability and interactivity can stabilize the grid's electrical supply and provide the asynchronous balance of supply and demand requirements [3], [4]. Figure 1: (a) global mean surface temperatures [5], and (b) daily curve energy duck-curve in California [6] Energy storage systems can be classified into electrochemical, mechanical, or thermal types [7]. Electrochemical energy storage typically uses batteries that consist of an electrolyte, an anode, and a cathode, where electrical energy is released or gained by the movement of ions from the anode to the cathode through the electrolyte during discharge and, when connected to a circuit, during recharge [8], typically used renewable energy sources such as wind or solar photovoltaics [9], [10]. Mechanical energy storage systems usually include liquid displacement systems, such as dams, which are beyond the scope of this study [7]. Thermal energy storage (TES) systems have significant potential in the US, particularly for space heating and cooling applications, given their substantial share in the built environment and the increasing adoption of dual-purpose (heating and cooling) heat pumps (HPs).
